title: The FBI Raids a County Election Office and Seizes the 2020 Ballots
facts: On January 28, 2026, the FBI raided the Fulton County, Georgia elections office and seized roughly 700 boxes of 2020 ballots, along with tabulator tapes, voter rolls, and electronic ballot images. ABC News called the seizure "apparently unprecedented."

Trump personally ordered Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to Atlanta. She was physically present at the raid, despite the DNI being barred by law from domestic law enforcement, and she put agents on speakerphone with Trump, who thanked them in what officials described as a "pep talk."
The warrant was premised on 2020 fraud claims that roughly 60 courts, Trump's own attorney general, and Georgia's Republican secretary of state had already rejected.
Fulton County called the warrant improper and is fighting in court to keep the materials in Georgia under seal.
take: Five years after an election he lost by 12,000 votes in the state, the president sent the FBI and his intelligence chief into the county that counted it. Whatever this is, it is not evidence-gathering. It is a demonstration to every election office in the country of what happens to jurisdictions he loses.

title: Intelligence Officials Take Puerto Rico's Voting Machines on a Venezuela Pretext
facts: In May 2025, DNI Tulsi Gabbard's office obtained Puerto Rico's voting machines, with the local U.S. attorney, Homeland Security Investigations, and the FBI facilitating the handover, to investigate claims that Venezuela had hacked them.
No evidence of Venezuelan interference was found. A later teardown found ordinary chips from China, Japan, South Korea, and Malaysia, no Venezuelan code, and no hacking.

Sen. Mark Warner: "Absent a foreign nexus, intelligence agencies have absolutely no lawful role in domestic election administration. This is exactly the kind of overreach Congress wrote the law to prevent."
Puerto Rico does not vote in presidential elections. Election experts read the episode as a test run for seizing machines somewhere that lacked the political power to resist.

title: Officials Tried to Ban the Voting Machines Half the Country Uses
facts: Reuters reported in May 2026 that Trump officials, led by White House election adviser Kurt Olsen, tried to ban Dominion voting machines used in roughly 27 states by having the Commerce Department declare their components a national security risk.
The goal was to force much of the country onto hand-counted paper ballots, potentially before the 2026 midterms. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was reportedly unaware of the discussions.

The plan failed because officials could not find legal grounds to declare the machines a threat. No U.S. voting machine has ever been shown to have been hacked in an election, and about 98% of jurisdictions already produce auditable paper records.
Election-security expert Alex Halderman: switching to hand counting "would be chaotic and might facilitate cheating."

The push resumed before the midterms. CNN reported on September 10, 2026 that Trump allies, "including some inside the administration," are pressing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to use his supply-chain authority to ban certain voting machines over Chinese-made components. Emails obtained by American Oversight show activists Will Huff and Conrad Reynolds discussed election security with Chief of Staff Susie Wiles in August 2025; she connected them with Ed Martin at the Justice Department, and they sent him a "Proposed Ban Plan."

Huff wrote to Martin: "This can immediately force states to move to hand-marked and hand-counted ballots like the President wishes." The activists said on their podcast that Lutnick met them for more than two hours in August 2026 and "said he would be getting on it." Commerce did not respond to CNN and has taken no action.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters in August 2026 warning that foreign-made components could "potentially compromise election infrastructure at any stage of the supply chain." Voting-system vendors told CNN that foreign parts are common across industries, and that paper records allow any result to be audited.

title: The Agency That Certifies Voting Systems Is Left With Nobody Home
facts: On July 9, 2026, Trump removed the last members of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission, firing Democrats Thomas Hicks and Benjamin Hovland while Republican Christy McCormick was allowed to resign. With zero commissioners, the agency cannot take official action until the Senate confirms replacements.

The EAC certifies voting systems, maintains the national voter registration form, distributes federal election funds, and advises election officials. In March 2025 Trump had ordered it to rewrite the national registration form to require documentary proof of citizenship.

Months earlier, the administration blocked appointments to the EAC's Technical Guidelines Development Committee, leaving nearly half its 15 seats vacant, unprecedented in its 20-year history, with no functioning body to update voting-system security guidelines before the midterms.
Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar: it "will again fall on Secretaries of State... to fill the gap."

title: The Supreme Court Lets the Mail-Voting Order Advance, Without Ruling It Legal
facts: On March 31, 2026, Trump signed an executive order directing DHS to compile federal lists of "confirmed U.S. citizens eligible to vote in each state" and giving the Postal Service control over mail ballot distribution. It was drafted in part by Kurt Olsen, who was involved in the 2020 election-overturn effort.

States refused immediately. New Hampshire's secretary of state: "The Federal Government cannot usurp New Hampshire's express constitutional authority." Twenty-three Democratic-led states sued; at least four lawsuits are pending.
The Constitution assigns election administration to the states (Article I, Section 4). Election expert David Becker predicted courts would block the order "before the ink is dry."

In May, U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee, declined to block it, reasoning that no agency had yet acted on it in a way that harmed the plaintiffs. By June, plaintiffs told an appeals court the order was already being implemented through the USPS rule and DHS memos.

On July 25, 2026, the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals (2-1) refused to lift a June 25 injunction blocking the order's key provisions in the 23 states, leaving the federal "citizenship list" and ballot-routing scheme blocked while the case proceeds.

On July 27, 2026, the DOJ took it to the Supreme Court, asking on the emergency docket to put the injunction on hold and let the order take effect in the 23 states and D.C., 99 days before the midterms. The Court ordered the states to respond by August 3. A single emergency order could decide whether the federal government screens the nation's mail ballots this fall.
Trump himself voted by mail in Florida three days before signing the order.

On August 24, 2026, the Supreme Court granted emergency applications from the DOJ and a dozen Republican-led states and lifted, 6-3, Judge Talwani's June injunction blocking the order in the 23 states and D.C. that sued.

The majority ruled on standing, not legality: any injury would come from "the downstream action that the Secretary might take in the future," which was "no more than conjecture." It added that its ruling "does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful."

A second, nationwide injunction Talwani issued August 11 in the League of Women Voters case was not before the Court and remains in force, so the order still cannot be implemented for November as of this update.

Sotomayor and Kagan dissented together, saying the decision "merely postpones adjudication." Jackson dissented separately: the ruling "needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections."

title: The Supreme Court Keeps the Post Office's Ballot-Refusal Rule Out of the Midterms
facts: Under the rule implementing Trump's mail-voting order, USPS would deliver mail ballots only for states that hand over their voter lists 60 or more days before the election and put a unique tracking barcode on every ballot. USPS could refuse noncompliant ballots.
On June 24, Postmaster General David Steiner confirmed under oath that USPS would not deliver ballots for states that refuse to hand over voter rolls: "Under our proposed regulation? No."
A district judge blocked the rule in early July. On July 17, a three-judge appeals panel temporarily lifted that injunction, letting the rule advance while litigation continues.
Implementation must happen before mid-September, when ballot mailing begins. Missing barcodes or mismatched records could delay or void ballots, hitting elderly, disabled, and rural voters hardest.

On August 11, 2026, a federal judge in Massachusetts issued a preliminary injunction barring USPS from implementing Section 3 of the executive order for the November elections, finding the provision likely unconstitutional.

On August 21, USPS issued its final rule implementing that same section anyway, effective immediately, stating it will be implemented "immediately" for the November elections if the injunctive orders are lifted.

Plaintiffs in League of Women Voters of Massachusetts v. Trump moved to enforce the court's order, asking the court to confirm the rule "has no force or effect" before November and to bar USPS from taking "no implementation or preparatory steps" this year.

The Supreme Court's August 24 order lifted the other injunction, the June one covering the suing states. The August 11 nationwide injunction that reaches this USPS rule survives. Election law professor Rick Hasen expects the trial court to amend it to bar implementation of the now-final rule outright.

The rule requires election officials to submit each mail voter's name and address to a new USPS portal, along with unique Intelligent Mail barcodes assigned to the envelopes used to send and return that voter's ballot.

Postal officials and election administrators warned in late August that the timing invites mismatched barcodes, incomplete records and technical failures across thousands of local election offices, any of which could stop an eligible voter from receiving a ballot. The objection is operational, not ideological.

On August 26, 2026, states sued to block the rule, two days after the Supreme Court lifted the other injunction. USPS still cannot implement it for November 3, because the nationwide injunction was not before the Court.

On August 27, 2026, Judge Talwani did exactly what Hasen predicted: she granted a 14-day temporary restraining order blocking the final rule, in the League of Women Voters case and in a parallel state case, finding the challengers likely to win both on unconstitutionality and on USPS lacking authority to issue the rule at all.

Talwani noted the administration had not offered "any evidence regarding fraudulent absentee or mail-in voting," and wrote that the government's interest in "correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement."

On the calendar, she found the states "have neither time nor funds" to redesign ballots, update election management systems, train staff on the USPS portal and upload voter data before the midterms, and that the administration gave "no reply" to the states' argument that compliance would be impossible for many of them.

A hearing on a longer-lasting preliminary injunction is set for September 3, 2026. The executive order's separate provision directing DHS to compile lists of eligible voters and send them to states was not blocked and remains in effect.

On September 1, 2026, Sen. Richard Blumenthal released a USPS official's account of how the ballot portal is being built. The whistleblower called the work "secretive, rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed," said USPS compressed into weeks a system that normally takes nine months to a year, and said testing procedures for the platform were eliminated to meet deadlines described as impossible.

The operational detail that matters most: according to the account, if a state delivers a batch of 10,000 ballots and USPS cannot match a single one against the portal, USPS would refuse to mail the other 9,999 and expect the state to take the whole batch back to fix the one.

The official warned that "potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner, or at all." Blumenthal's letter also alleges USPS kept building the portal while injunctions barred implementation, describing a "pattern of defiance of court orders." USPS has not publicly rebutted the technical claims.

On September 4, 2026, after a hearing the day before, Judge Indira Talwani replaced her August 27 temporary restraining order with a preliminary injunction. It blocks the mandatory Outbound and Return Federal Ballot Mail Envelope Standards, mandatory registration for the Postal Service Federal Ballot Mail Portal, mandatory voter enrollment in that portal, and parts of the Outbound Federal Ballot Mail Verification procedures. The plaintiffs are the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts and a multistate group led by California.

Talwani's reasoning was structural: "Congress has never delegated its Elections Clause power to the USPS." She found the rule "clashes with Congress's statutory scheme, and is unconstitutional where it intrudes not only on Congress's Elections Clause powers but also that power left to the States."

On the timing she wrote that implementation "less than seventy days before the November 2026 election threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail," while "the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation of the Final Rule."

The administration moved twice in two days. On September 5 the Justice Department asked the First Circuit for a stay. On September 6 Solicitor General John Sauer took it to the Supreme Court, seeking a stay pending appeal and an administrative stay, describing the rule as imposing "only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements for federal-election ballots sent via U.S. Mail." Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson ordered responses by 4 p.m. Eastern on Wednesday, September 9.
North Carolina and Alabama began mailing ballots as early as September 4, 2026, which is the clock the filings are racing.

On September 9, the day responses were due, Republican secretaries of state from Kentucky, North Dakota, South Dakota, Georgia, New Hampshire and Kansas, with Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson and 26 local election officials in Georgia and Utah, asked the Supreme Court not to let the rule take effect for the midterms. They took no position on its legality, only on timing: "late changes breed confusion, that confusion keeps eligible voters from voting, and that a chaotic election erodes confidence in the result," and "in many respects, the election is already underway." Federal law requires states to send ballots to military and overseas voters by September 19.

A Florida county previewed the envelope review. Leon County voluntarily submitted its outgoing ballot envelope, and on September 2 USPS rejected it because two lines were 0.236 of an inch apart instead of a quarter inch. After an initial denial on appeal, USPS approved the design on September 10. The county had used the same envelopes for tens of thousands of ballots in 2024 and the 2026 primary, and plans to mail roughly 32,000 ballots by Florida's September 24 deadline. Supervisor of Elections Mark Earley: "The chaos factor is the real problem."

On September 14, 2026, the Supreme Court denied the administration's request to let the rule take effect for November, saying "The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court's preliminary injunction." Justices Alito and Thomas dissented. Justice Kavanaugh wrote that the rule may fall within the Postal Service's authority, but that applying it in 2026 would be arbitrary and capricious "because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections." The order covers only this year's elections.

Shortly before, Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee in Washington, separately blocked the rule: "No statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule." He found the government "does not point to any record evidence that there will be significant fraud in the upcoming elections." Trump said the justices "are merely a shell of their original selves."

Trump's fuller post the next morning called the order "a big loss for Republicans, and America itself," saying it "makes cheating by the Radical Left 'Dumocrats,' on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do," and that "This Supreme Court is bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left." CBS News reported Trump himself voted by mail in Florida this year.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said the administration would comply, but that "President Trump's efforts to make sure that we have free and fair elections are not going to stop just in November or after or thereafter. So I expect you're going to see that work continue."

On September 17, 2026, Postmaster General David Steiner told the Associated Press the Postal Service had stopped building the system. "There's an injunction so we're not doing anything," he said. A memo to all postal employees the previous day said the agency would "not be enforcing any of these new rules in the 2026 federal election," and that "First and foremost, for Election Mail it is business as usual."

Steiner said he had planned to launch the citizenship-check portal around September 15. He also said the Postal Service will keep pushing states toward barcoded ballot envelopes in future cycles through pricing rather than a mandate: "If you use the barcode in the envelope, we'll charge you a lower price. If you don't, we're going to charge you a higher price." The scheme is paused for this election, not abandoned.
take: The legal fight and the practical one have separated, and the practical one now has a number attached. Talwani blocked the rule on both the law and the calendar, and a postal official has since described a system built in weeks instead of a year with its testing removed. Note what the batch rule would do if it holds: one unmatched record does not delay one ballot, it returns ten thousand. Whether the rule survives appeal matters less to November than whether the machinery behind it works at all, and the people building it are saying it does not.

title: The DOJ Sues 30 States for Voter Files and Loses Twenty-One Straight Times
facts: Trump's DOJ has filed roughly 30 lawsuits against 29 states plus D.C. demanding voter registration data: names, addresses, birthdates, partial Social Security numbers, and driver's license numbers, using a Civil Rights Act provision written to protect Black voters.

It is 0-for-21 in court, with no wins, losing every resolved case. Twelve of the losses came from judges appointed by Republican presidents, eight of them Trump's own. Trump appointee Judge Mary McElroy called the Rhode Island demand a "fishing expedition"; Judge Lance Walker in Maine noted an executive order contradicted DOJ assurances that no national database was being built.
Twelve Republican-led states complied voluntarily, so the data campaign advances even as it loses in court.
An NBC News review found the DOJ still cannot substantiate Trump's claims of widespread voter fraud months before the midterms.

On July 29, 2026, U.S. District Judge Zahid Quraishi dismissed the DOJ's demand for New Jersey's unredacted voter rolls, its eighteenth straight loss, noting that judges in more than a dozen other states had reached the same conclusion.

On August 3, 2026, U.S. District Judge Philip Brimmer, a George W. Bush appointee, dismissed the DOJ's demand for Colorado's voter rolls with prejudice, its twentieth straight loss; the nineteenth was a dismissal in Illinois. The department has also lost the only appellate ruling so far.

On August 6-7, 2026, U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss dismissed the DOJ's demand for the District of Columbia's full voter list, its twenty-first straight loss; a Washington State case argued August 4 was still undecided. The DOJ has appealed 16 of the losses, and the 6th Circuit has already rejected one (Michigan).

In early September 2026, Georgia released an audit of roughly 7.9 million voter registrations. It found the rolls more than 99.9% accurate with no evidence of malicious manipulation, and estimated that no more than 0.1% of records would have allowed a vote despite an unverified identity, invalid address, or citizenship problem.

The audit did find errors: about 2,570 potential noncitizens had at some point been placed in active or inactive status, 407 of them with a voting history. Auditors traced the cause to coding mistakes in the Department of Driver Services licensing process and to county verification failures, not to intentional registration by noncitizens.
Georgia joins nearly two dozen states that have run similar reviews over the past two years and found scant evidence of noncitizen voting at a scale capable of changing outcomes.

On September 1 and 2, 2026, reporting described a planned federal voter fraud inquiry in Georgia, and DHS subpoenaed voter files from Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger. The subpoena sought 13 files. Gabe Sterling, Raffensperger's director of special projects, called that relatively modest against Georgia's eight million-plus voters and said other states had received similar requests.

DHS cited more than 24,000 cases flagged by the SAVE system as potential noncitizens on voter rolls since April 2025. A federal court vacated the rebuilt SAVE system as unlawful in June 2026, and when Virginia checked its own SAVE flags, 94% of the people identified as noncitizens were U.S. citizens.

title: A National Voter Database Nobody Authorized
facts: CNN reported in April 2026 that the administration is building a national voter database through a DOJ-DHS data sharing deal, with 50 to 60 million voter records already collected from states, assembled through executive channels with no congressional authorization.

The DHS SAVE system it relies on flagged about 21,000 of 60 million records as possible noncitizens, 0.00035%. In Virginia's experience with the same system, 94% of people flagged as "noncitizens" were actually U.S. citizens.
Experts warn naturalized citizens are the people most likely to be wrongly caught in the net.

As of February 2026, 27 states had agreed to run their voter rolls through the revamped SAVE system against Social Security and passport data. DHS acknowledges "the SAVE Program may produce inaccurate results," and has had to correct information it gave at least five states after the system misidentified voters as noncitizens.

On June 22, 2026, U.S. District Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan vacated the rebuilt SAVE system and its privacy notices as contrary to law, arbitrary and capricious, in excess of statutory authority, and adopted without required procedure, finding violations of the Privacy Act, the Social Security Act and the Administrative Procedure Act. Her opinion said the agencies "haphazardly combined and repurposed the private information of millions of Americans, including citizenship data that they knew to be unreliable."

The vacatur did not settle it. On July 7, 2026, U.S. District Judge T. Kent Wetherell II granted an emergency motion by Florida, Ohio, Iowa and Indiana to enforce a settlement with DHS, and a judge ordered the tool restored the next day. Two federal courts were issuing conflicting orders about the same system.

Trump's March 2026 executive order contains a section, separate from the mail-ballot provisions that have been litigated all year, directing federal agencies to compile and send each state's chief election official a list of individuals confirmed to be citizens aged 18 or older, no fewer than 60 days before each federal election.

On September 1, 2026, DHS published a "State Citizenship Lists Portal" webpage saying the lists were coming soon. A June DHS memo had set a target of having it fully functional by Friday, September 4.

The lists are not built from state voter registration files. They are assembled from federal databases whose citizenship information is incomplete, which is why plaintiffs argue actual citizens will be left off.

On September 1, 2026, the Electronic Privacy Information Center sued DHS and the Social Security Administration in federal court in Maryland, represented by Protect Democracy and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington. The 41-page complaint cites the Privacy Act of 1974, the Social Security Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, and the constitutional allocation of election authority to the states.

The complaint alleges DHS is "aggressively pushing state election officials to use this admittedly unreliable data to purge their voter rolls of purported non-citizens, under threat of fines, penalties, and even prison time."

EPIC deputy director John Davisson: "Building a database containing the identities, Social Security numbers, addresses, and citizenship information of every U.S. citizen is an extraordinary illegal overreach."
No ruling had issued as of September 3, 2026.

title: A Whistleblower Says DHS Officers Were Told to Pose as Voters to Search State Voter Records
facts: A federal whistleblower's disclosure, published September 14, 2026 by Sens. Chuck Schumer and Alex Padilla, alleges that a DHS program called the "Unlawful Voter Initiative" directed USCIS employees to pose as individual voters to access their records on state voter-lookup websites. The report says the program "has potentially already committed thousands of violations of state law."

According to the report, officers had a quota of 40 people a day, "giving officers only twelve minutes to determine if a subject is a U.S. citizen," and training material acknowledged "there will be U.S. citizens in this population." Officers who raised legal concerns were told they were "not personally liable."

DHS said it "accessed publicly available data from states' voter rolls and cross referenced them with known aliens in our systems." The claims are allegations; no court, inspector general or state has confirmed the searches broke state law.

On September 17, 2026, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin saying the department may have violated several state laws, and demanded it preserve access logs, correspondence and training materials. Virginia's voter-lookup tool is limited to people who attest under penalty of law that they are searching their own record, and Jones wrote that "Virginia Election Code does not permit disclosure of this protected information to the federal government without a court order."

The Associated Press reported that USCIS staff were made in late August to drop other work, complete a training of under two hours, and begin running department-supplied lists through state voter registration systems at roughly 40 people per day. DHS had not responded at publication, and no court has ruled.

Part of the account now has sworn support. In a September 14 court filing, a senior official in the immigration agency's fraud unit swore that the unit "has been investigating potential illegal voting by aliens who are not lawfully permitted to vote" and had used Social Security Administration data to help determine "whether illegal voting may have occurred." The filing does not address officers posing as voters on state websites. title: Six Weeks Before the Election, Three News Organizations Are Barred From the White House
facts: On September 18, 2026 Trump posted that "effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW... and Politico... from the White House as a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" Three named reporters and at least two camera operators were turned away, and CBS News witnessed part of it. No written notice or explanation was given, and the White House press office has issued no statement of its own.

Under Sherrill v. Knight, the 1977 case governing White House credentials, access cannot be denied based on the content of coverage, and any denial requires notice, a chance to respond and a decision in writing. Trump cited no specific article and said the ban could be lifted if the outlets "could straighten themselves out." Asked whether it would survive court review, he said, "I don't think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day."

On September 21 the three outlets said they were filing suit that day in federal court in Washington on due process and First Amendment grounds; the case, Cable News Network, Inc. v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-03287, was filed that day and assigned to Judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee who ruled for CNN in the 2018 Jim Acosta pass case. A hearing on restoring the passes is set for September 23. The night before, at 10:55 p.m., the White House removed CNN as the next day's television pool network, including Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly. That morning Trump gave a rationale he had not used before, writing of what he calls the fake news, "It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!"

Print, radio and photo pools continued, and the networks still cover open events with their own crews.

title: Trump Promises a $5,000 'Trump Dividend' to Every Adult if Republicans Keep Congress
facts: At the Republican Party's first midterm convention, in Dallas on September 9, 2026, Trump said: "If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them, because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000." He added, "So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000. It will be called 'the Trump dividend.'"

He named no funding source or mechanism. Vice President Vance said within the hour that tariffs would pay for it and that it would be limited to the middle class, a limit Trump did not state. Sen. Bernie Moreno said he would have a bill ready "immediately after the November 3rd election." Congress would have to appropriate the money.

With roughly 240 to 245 million adult citizens, the promise costs about $1.2 trillion or more. Tariff revenue was about $154.5 billion in the first ten months of fiscal 2026, and the Supreme Court's February tariff ruling has forced more than $100 billion in refunds. The deficit is running near $1.8 trillion.

Election-law scholar Rick Hasen wrote that the pledge is "almost certainly protected by the First Amendment" as a campaign promise delivered through the normal processes of government. Rep. Chip Roy asked how it would be paid for; former Freedom Caucus chairman Bob Good called it a "socialist vote-buying scheme."
Trump's earlier $5,000 DOGE dividend (February 2025) and $2,000 tariff dividend (November 2025) were never paid.

Asked on September 10 by CBS News Texas whether Congress would have to approve the payments, Trump said: "Well, we think not. I think they will do it if we needed it. But we think not." CBS reported it is not clear what legal authority a president would have to make payments that could cost upwards of a trillion dollars without Congress.

Asked the same night by Fox News host Laura Ingraham why he did not simply pay it now, Trump said: "Because they can't. I'll tell you what, because the Democrats can't do it, because with them it's negative growth." Republicans currently control both chambers.

Asked by ABC's Rachel Scott why a strong economy would need "an incentive for people to turn out to vote," Trump said it was "a reward for people having to put up with five years and four years of a horrible situation caused by Biden." Two nights earlier he had tied it to the result: "So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000."

On September 13, outside Air Force One, Trump said, "The $5,000 is going to happen 100 percent," and explained why it would not come sooner: "I don't want to do it now, because if the Democrats get it, our country will be in shambles and they won't be able to do it." Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the administration could "earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers," while National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett suggested it could move through a reconciliation package in Congress.

Asked on September 10 where the money would come from, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick pointed to the Trump Platinum Card, a $5 million visa program that has not launched: "We have a waitlist of more than 100,000 people who want to come. That's $500 billion." Newsweek noted a place on the waitlist is not revenue and that 100,000 payments would cover about 41 percent of the estimated $1.23 trillion cost.
take: This is not vote-buying in the legal sense, and the tracker does not call it that. It is something the law has not had to think about: a sitting president conditioning a cash payment to the public on which party wins an election, with no money to pay it. Whether a voter believes the check is coming is the whole point, and the record on the last two dividends answers that. The card is here because the promise is itself an instrument aimed at the outcome, made by the man whose administration is also setting the rules for the count.

title: Trump Leads a Raised-Hand Pledge to 'the Greatest President' That Included 'Cheat Like Hell Like They Do'
facts: Closing the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on September 10, 2026, Trump asked the arena to raise their right hands and repeat a pledge "to the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can't even breathe." The pledge he led included the line, "I don't care if I'm registered or not, I'm going to try to cheat like hell like they do. There has never been bigger cheaters." It closed with "So help me God," and he added, "You know what happens if you don't vote? You go to hell."

Per Mediaite's transcript, the crowd repeated the lines praising Trump and the closing oath, but the transcript shows no crowd response to the "cheat like hell" line. The Hill reported "some in the crowd tried to repeat" the pledge amid laughter. Headlines saying Trump made supporters swear or vow to cheat go further than the transcript supports.

"Like they do" refers to Democrats. Moments earlier Trump said Democrats oppose voter ID "because they want to cheat." CNN's fact check found no basis for broadly describing Democrats as election cheaters. Whether he meant his own line as sarcasm or literally has not been clarified by Trump or the White House.
The pledge came at an event where Trump was campaigning for voter ID and proof-of-citizenship requirements.
take: Read as a joke about Democrats, the line still does what the fraud claims elsewhere on this page do: it tells a crowd, from the stage and weeks before the vote, that the other side cheats. Read literally, it tells supporters registration does not matter. The White House has not said which reading it intends, and both point at the same November.

title: The Census Bureau Claims 24,000 Noncitizens Voted in 2020, and Trump Declares 'I WON THE ELECTION!'
facts: On August 18, 2026, the Census Bureau released a report claiming more than 24,000 noncitizens illegally voted in 2020, from an analysis of 128 million voter records. Trump posted "I WON THE ELECTION!" and predicted the number would "explode." Taken at face value, 24,000 votes would be less than 0.02 percent of the roughly 160 million ballots cast.

CNN, citing three former bureau officials who served under Trump, reported that the administration had installed partisan analysts from the Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute inside the bureau, and NPR reported the analysis was not done by career civil servants.
The next day, in a revision dated August 19, the Commerce Department removed language banning political interference from its scientific integrity policy, NPR reported.

title: Trump Says the Iran War 'Will End Immediately After Our Election'
facts: At Joint Base Andrews on September 9, 2026, before flying to the Republican midterm convention, Trump said: "I think the war is going to end immediately after the election. They can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice, weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon."

Asked whether negotiations would resume, he said, "We're not looking for it, to be honest." In Dallas that night he said Iran was "hanging out for dear life, hoping that we lose, so they can deal with dumb, weak Democrats."

The remarks came on a day Iran said it had targeted ten ships near the Strait of Hormuz, including two U.S. vessels, after U.S. forces destroyed five Iranian tankers. Newsweek counted roughly 23 separate Trump predictions since February of when the war would end.
An NBC News Decision Desk poll found 69 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the war. A Reuters/Ipsos survey put his approval at 33 percent.

At the same stop, asked how he would explain oil prices that had just reached highs not seen since the war's early weeks, Trump said, "Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward." He predicted gas would fall below $2 a gallon but said, "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm." Brent crude traded above $101 a barrel that day for the first time since July.
take: A president is free to argue that an adversary wants him to lose. What this statement does is tie the end of a war he began without a vote of Congress to the date of a domestic election, in his own words, and cast the opposition party as the enemy's preferred outcome. Read alongside the impeachment card above it, it is the president's own account of what November decides.

title: Kimmel Keeps a Senate Candidate Off Broadcast TV, Citing Threats From Trump's FCC
facts: On September 9, 2026, Jimmy Kimmel announced that his interview with James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Texas, would be posted to YouTube and would not air on ABC. On air, he said: "His FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don't like."

No FCC order barred the interview. Kimmel said the decision was made "out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas." After Talarico appeared on ABC's The View in February, the FCC opened an inquiry into ABC's Houston station and 20 Texas ABC affiliates filed equal-time notices.

In January 2026 the FCC's Media Bureau said late-night and daytime talk shows could no longer assume they qualify for the equal-time rule's news-interview exemption. CBS lawyers kept Talarico off Stephen Colbert's broadcast in February on the same basis. Disney and ABC sued the FCC in August; a hearing on the FCC's motion to dismiss is set for the week of October 5.

Kimmel noted he had interviewed candidates for 20 years, including Trump in 2015 and 2016, and said: "In the America we live in right now, that is the best that we can do until November." The FCC did not respond to requests for comment.
take: The regulator never had to rule. It only had to make the cost of airing a Senate candidate uncertain enough that two of the three largest broadcast networks decided not to find out. That is how a chilling effect works, and this one lands eight weeks before an election in a state where the same candidate is on the ballot.

title: The Redistricting War Has Moved 34.8 Million Americans Into New Districts
facts: A September 17, 2026 report by the nonprofit Protect Democracy found that 34.8 million people, about one in ten Americans, now live in a different congressional district than they did during the 2024 cycle. About one-fifth of Americans live in a district where more than a quarter of the electorate is new.

Both the Associated Press and Democracy Docket trace the origin to Trump. AP wrote that the battle "began when Trump urged the Republican-controlled legislature in Texas, the second most populous state, to redraw its congressional map to help the party." California responded in kind and the practice spread; Democracy Docket counts at least nine states that have redistricted since 2024.
Redrawing maps between censuses is legal but was close to taboo. Per Pew Research, in the past 50 years a state redrew its map outside the normal ten-year cycle only twice before this round.

Missouri shows how unsettled the maps still are. As of September 19, overseas ballots had gone out under the state's 2022 map while Republicans asked the Eighth Circuit to restore the 2025 map drawn at Trump's urging; the court had not ruled, the Missouri Independent reported.
take: Gerrymandering is old and bipartisan. What is new is the tempo. When maps can be redrawn any time the party in power wants a better result, the district stops being a place and becomes a bid, and the voter stops choosing the representative. Protect Democracy calls it a doom loop; the arithmetic is that one in ten Americans had their district changed between elections without moving house.

title: The President Says the Super PAC's Billion Dollars Is 'My Money That I Control'
facts: Federal law bars a federal officeholder from directing the spending of an organization that accepts unlimited contributions. On September 14, 2026 the Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the Federal Election Commission against Trump, the super PAC MAGA Inc. and its treasurer under that provision, 52 U.S.C. § 30125(e)(1)(A).

The evidence is almost entirely Trump's own public statements. Corrected by an interviewer who described the money as belonging to his allies, he said, "Not my allies, I control it." In the Oval Office on September 4 he said, "I think I have like close to a billion dollars in the super PAC, and I'm allocating probably $400, $500 million," and, asked how he decides, "How do I make it? I sit down and I say, 'let's do this, let's do that.'" He also said: "this is money from MAGA Inc. This is my money that I control."

MAGA Inc. calls the complaint "frivolous" and says it "fully complies with the law." A complaint is an allegation, not a finding, and this one is unlikely to become either: the Federal Election Commission has two of six commissioners confirmed, too few to hold a formal meeting. Meanwhile MAGA Inc. has reported $10 million spent on the Texas Senate race, with nearly $140 million more reserved by related committees.
take: The soft-money rule exists so that an officeholder cannot personally direct unlimited money into their own party's races. Whether Trump broke it is for an agency that cannot currently convene to decide. What is not in dispute is that he described the arrangement the rule forbids, out loud, more than once, in the belief that saying so cost him nothing.
